newsitem.title: USA: NYC reaches drinking water pact with upstate towns.
newsitem.headline: NYC reaches drinking water pact with upstate towns.

text.p: New York City and state officials, saying they had overcome decades of mistrust between upstate and downstate communities, on Tuesday said they had reached a plan to protect the city's drinking water.
The stakes were high for the city, which hopes the new $340 million agreement will let it avoid building a $4 billion to $6 billion filtration system.

Mayor Rudolph Giuliani, in prepared remarks released at a news conference, said such a system would have doubled or tripled rate-payers' water bills. Instead, these bills will rise $7 a year for the next five years under the new plan.

The New York City water system each day supplies 1.4 billion gallons of water to eight million city residents and one million people who live in three counties north of the city. The water comes from 19 reservoirs that are located in a watershed that extends 125 miles north and west of the city.

Upstate communities, whose lands were flooded to create some of the reservoirs, have strenuously objected to the city's attempts to protect its water supplies by restricting development, which can cause pollution.

Under the new plan, New York City agreed to spend $260 million to buy more watershed lands and conservation easements to provide a buffer area around reservoirs, streams and wetlands. A fair market price will be paid for the land and the city cannot take it using the right of emminent domain.

Pataki, who has begun campaigning for a $1.75 billion environmental bond act, which goes to the voters in November, reiterated one of his Adminisration's key tenents, saying that environmental protection and economic growth are compatible.

"This historic agreement is the product of hard work, determination and a deep commitment by all sides to protect the drinking water for millions of New Yorkers and the economic vitality of the watershed communities," Pataki said.
New York City also will spend another $82 million to start upgrading the last three of the city's nine wastewater treatment plants in the watershed.
And it will "commit to fund" about $334 million in new protection and partnership programs with local communities over the next decade.

Both Giuliani and Gov. George Pataki, who have had a difficult relationship though both are Republicans, praised each other's leadership, noting the final talks, which began about 10 months ago, had been a lengthy and thorny process.
"This is a model really for the future," Giuliani told reporters.

While the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA), which helped bring the parties together, plans to again waive a requirement that the city build a filtration system, New York City will remain under the gun.

"To prepare for all the contingencies, New York City will continue on a dual track," said Carol Browner, explaining the city still has to draft a filtration plan to ensure that it is ready if the federal agency determines it is needed.
Browner also promised that the EPA will strictly monitor how the pact is put in place, to ensure the public health.

The agreement now goes before the public, which will have 60 days to make comments, and one environmental group, the Natural Resources Defense Council (NRDC), which had criticized the preliminary pact, is expected to review it carefully. The group elected not to participate in the final talks as some of the issues it had raised appeared to be closed, making their input too late, said an industry source, who declined to be named.
Questions about whether New York City will have adequate control of how its funds are spent also might be raised.
Robert Kennedy, Jr., chief prosecuting attorney for Hudson RiverKeeper, an environmental group, who participated in the negotiations, made it clear that the job is not over yet.
"It is a great agreement but it is far from perfect and it's going to take years and years of work," he told reporters.
